methods.name: block.close
methods.description: Close a block within a session. The response's `revision` is the session structural revision after the mutation, unchanged when the mutation is a no-op.
validation_notes: Returns the closed `block_id` and the session revision produced by its removal.
Runs the same close lifecycle path as a block-emitted close action; it does not detach the block.
Fails if `block_id` does not identify a live block in the session.
Fails with not found if `session_id` does not identify a live session.

methods.name: block.event
methods.description: Deliver an external event to a block within a session.
validation_notes: The event envelope uses a tagged `type` + `payload` JSON shape.
Returns an empty result value.

methods.name: block.method
methods.description: Invoke a typed method on a block within a session and return its result.
validation_notes: `method` selects the logical block method to call; the detailed block-creator section below lists the methods each creator exposes.
`args` is passed through to the target block method unchanged and is validated by that method's own schema.
The result schema depends on the selected block method, so this dispatcher has no single output schema of its own.

Requests to this method can run at the same time as other requests, including `client.key`. To call a block method or block action bound to a key, use `client.action`, which runs in order with `client.key`.

methods.name: block_creator.list
methods.description: List configured block creators and their advertised constructible flavors.
validation_notes: The request body may be omitted entirely because the method takes no arguments.
`flavor` is the fully-qualified value accepted by `block` layout leaves and `session.new_block`.

A method's `actions` are things a person can do with a block of that type, such as by choosing them from a command palette or pressing a bound key. An action's full name is the creator name, a dot, and its `name`, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.reset`. Performing an action calls its method with `args`. These are fixed argument values, not a schema. An action without `args` calls the method with no arguments.
Returns the server's configured static creator catalog; custom SessionSetup hooks without a matching Config.Creators catalog may produce an empty list.

methods.name: client.action
methods.description: Perform an action as the calling client. The action can come from the account's configuration file or from a block type.
validation_notes: The action name determines what runs. A name without a dot, such as `dev_layout`, is an action defined with `rex.action` in the config file, and `args` is passed to it. A name that starts with a block type's creator name, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.reset` or `com.superlogical.terminal.write`, is an action or method of that block type. `client.keymap` lists all of these names in `actions`.

An action that a block type declares, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.reset`, has fixed arguments. A request for one that includes `args` fails with `bad_request`. A block method, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.write`, takes its input from `args`.
Client actions, such as `pane.split`, are performed by the client and cannot be sent here. A request for one, or for any name the server does not know, fails with `not_found`.

Requests to this method and to `client.key` run one at a time, in the order they arrive on the connection. Use this method, not `block.method`, for an action bound to a key, so the action takes effect after the keys typed before it.

`ordered_after` is the ID of the ordered request that the connection handled just before this one. It is omitted if this was the first ordered request on the connection. Use it to check the order. For example, if you send a `client.key` request and then this request, `ordered_after` is the `client.key` request's ID.

The action runs as the calling connection's client. A block action requires `session_id`, and the connection must be attached to that session. The action runs on `block_id`, or on the session's focused block if `block_id` is omitted. If that block is not of the action's block type, the request fails with `conflict`.

An action from the config file may omit `session_id`. It then sees no `ctx.session_id`, and its session API calls have no default session. With `session_id`, it sees `block_id`, or the focused block, as `ctx.block_id`.
`origin` is `key`, `palette`, or `api`, and defaults to `api`. Actions from the config file read it as `ctx.origin`. The value `script` is reserved for actions called with `rex.invoke`.
`result` is the block method's result, or the value returned by the config file's action. It is omitted if that action returned nothing, `nil`, or `true`.

`client_actions` lists the actions the config file's action asked this client to perform with `rex.client.queue`, in order. After the response arrives, perform each one as you would a key binding with the same action and arguments.

If a config file action raises an error, the message starts with its location, such as `init.lua:4: attempt to index a nil value`. If it runs too long, the request fails with `timeout`. If the config file is reloaded while it runs, the request fails with `conflict`. In both cases, some of the action may already have run.

`servers` lists the other servers this client is connected to, such as `[{"name": "studio", "id": "srv-1"}]`. A config file action can send an API call to one of them with `rex.server(name)`. Names must be non-empty and unique, and IDs must be non-empty. Do not list the server you are sending the request to. The server does not interpret either value. A request that breaks these rules fails with `bad_request`.

`server` is the name of the server in `servers` that owns `session_id` and `block_id`. Omit it when the session belongs to the server you are sending the request to. When `server` is set, the IDs are passed to the action unchanged. They are not checked, the connection does not need to be attached to the session, and the focused block is not filled in, so send `block_id` yourself. The action reads the name as `ctx.server`, and its `rex.session.*`, `rex.block.call`, and `rex.call` calls go to that server. A block action with `server` set fails with `bad_request`. Send it to the server that owns the block instead.

When the action calls another server, this connection receives a `client_call_requested` event with `call_id`, `server` (the server's `id`), `method`, and `args`. Make the call on that server, then report the outcome with `client.reply` on this connection. The action waits up to 10 seconds for each reply. If no reply arrives in time, or the reply is an error, the action's call returns an error, as a failed call to this server would, and the action keeps running. A reply that arrives too late fails with `not_found`.

An action from the config file may run for 30 seconds in total, including the time it spends waiting for other servers. If it runs longer, the request fails with `timeout`. A key handler in the config file may run for 5 seconds. Clients cannot change these limits.

methods.name: client.inspect
methods.description: Describe one client connected to the server, including its actions.
validation_notes: `client_id` can name any client, not only the one that sends the request.
A request without a valid `client_id` fails with `bad_request`. An ID that names no connected client fails with `not_found`, including the ID of a client that has left.
`actions` lists the actions the client declared in its most recent `client.keymap` request. The field is left out when the client has declared none.
To ask the client to perform one of these actions, call `client.perform`.

methods.name: client.key
methods.description: Send a key through the client's script bindings and the account's configuration file, then to a block.

key.description: Physical key, named after the W3C UI Events KeyboardEvent code in snake_case. A key outside the list below is named "unidentified".

mods.description: Active modifiers joined with "+" in the order "shift", "ctrl", "alt", "super", "caps_lock", "num_lock", "shift_side", "ctrl_side", "alt_side", "super_side". The empty string means no modifier is active.

consumed_mods.description: Active modifiers joined with "+" in the order "shift", "ctrl", "alt", "super", "caps_lock", "num_lock", "shift_side", "ctrl_side", "alt_side", "super_side". The empty string means no modifier is active.

action.description: Whether the key was pressed, released, or is repeating while held down.

validation_notes: This method is ordered. It shares one queue with the connection's other ordered methods, and each request finishes before the next begins, which is what keeps typed keys in sequence.

`block_id` names the target block directly. Omit it and the key goes to the session's focused block, read once before the script bindings run. Either way the scripts see the block the key will actually reach.

`handled` reports that the scripts consumed the key, in which case no block received it. It stays false when no script is loaded, when no exclusive binding claimed the key, and when there was no block to fall through to.
Only the keys `client.set_script` and `client.keymap` report reach the scripts at all. Every other key goes straight to the block.

`prefix` lists the keys pressed before `key` when `key` completes a key sequence. For ctrl+b followed by x, send x as `key` and `["ctrl+b"]` as `prefix`. Send it when you complete a sequence the keymap binds to `client.key.forward`, and omit it for a key pressed on its own.
A key with a `prefix` reaches only the functions bound to that exact sequence. A key without one reaches only the functions bound to that key alone.
The server does not remember keys between requests, so send the whole sequence once, when it is complete. If no function takes the key, only `key` goes on to the block. The keys in `prefix` never do.
A request fails with `bad_request` if an element of `prefix` is not a valid key binding. The error names the element.

methods.name: client.keymap
methods.description: Resolve this client's keymap from its own layers, the config file, and its own script.
validation_notes: The answer stacks the caller's `defaults` at the bottom, then the account's config file and the script this connection installed with `client.set_script`, and the caller's `overrides` on top of all of it. Each list is read bottom first, so its first layer is its lowest.

Every layer is read in bind order: a later binding sits above an earlier one on the same key. Bindings come back the other way round, top of the stack first, which is the order a client should try them in.

A layer needs a `name`, unique across both lists and free of colons, which is reserved for the `file:line` a config reports. The name is what the layer's bindings report as their `source`, so a request that breaks one of those rules is refused rather than answered. A `source` inside a request is ignored.

Nothing about a `defaults` layer is ever reported, because it is what the client shipped with and the person asking cannot edit it. A stale removal or an unknown action in an `overrides` layer comes back as a warning whose source is that layer's name.

`keys` holds one key, or a key sequence as one key per element, such as `["ctrl+b", "c"]` for ctrl+b followed by c. The config file writes that sequence as `ctrl+b>c`, but a reply always lists the keys separately. A sequence sits on the stack of its first key, among that key's other bindings, in the same order. When the top binding a client can perform is a sequence, the client waits for the next key instead of acting. Waiting is the client's job, and the server keeps no state between keys.

A sequence bound to a Lua function comes back as a binding for `client.key.forward` with all of its keys. When a client completes the sequence, it sends the last key to `client.key` with the earlier keys in `prefix`. Like any forwarded binding, it is always available and ends its stack, but only for that exact sequence. Other sequences that start with the same key can still be reached.

A key that has both a binding of its own and a sequence that starts with it can only do what the higher of the two asks. The server keeps both bindings in the reply and adds one warning per key that names the binding that cannot run and the one above it. The warning's `source`, `action` and `key` are those of the binding that cannot run. It is reported even when that binding is a default, as long as the binding above it is not.
A removal takes off only the bindings whose keys it names in full. Removing `["ctrl+b"]` leaves every sequence that starts with ctrl+b, and removing `["ctrl+b", "c"]` leaves ctrl+b.

A key spelling this server cannot parse is carried through as written, in either list, so a newer client keeps its keys. Only a removal spelling the key the same way can take it off. A sequence with any element this server cannot parse is carried the same way, and takes no part in the warning above.

A binding or removal with a `mode` belongs to that mode. A mode is a named set of bindings that the client uses only while the mode is active. The config file writes a key in a mode as `resize/left`. A mode name contains only lowercase letters, digits, `_` and `-`, and `root` is reserved. A request with an invalid mode name is refused.
Bindings in a mode stack and are checked like any other bindings. A key in a mode never hides the same key outside the mode, and a removal only affects its own mode.

`modes` lists every mode in the keymap, sorted by name, and is omitted when there are none. A mode is listed if any layer binds a key in it, removes a key from it, or declares it with `rex.mode`. When `exclusive` is true, keys the mode does not bind are ignored while the mode is active. `blocked` lists keys that must not reach the bindings outside the mode while it is active. A removal in a mode that names no action always blocks its key, whether or not it removed anything, and never warns. One that names an action never blocks.

A removal with a `mode` and no `keys` removes the whole mode: every binding in it, every key it blocks and every declaration of it in the layers beneath. It blocks nothing and must not name an action. A mode with nothing left is not listed in `modes`. A higher layer that binds a key in the mode or declares it brings it back with only what that layer and those above it say. A client may send one in either list, and the config file writes one as `rex.unbind{ mode = "resize" }`.

The client decides which mode is active, using its own `client.mode.enter`, `client.mode.exit` and `client.mode.exit_all` actions. The server keeps no mode state. It warns about a binding of `client.mode.enter` whose `name` is not a mode in the keymap, and about a declared mode with nothing bound in it. A diagnostic about something in a mode names that mode in `mode`.
An omitted `actions` list turns off the warning for a binding that names an action the client does not have. A caller that wants the config file's bindings alone sends an empty request.

When `actions` is not empty, the server adds its own actions to it: those the config file defines with `rex.action`, every block method, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.write`, and every action a block type declares, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.reset`. A binding to one of these is never reported as unknown.

A binding to one of the server's own actions also has its arguments checked. Wrong arguments produce a warning at the binding's source, and the binding is kept. A block method's arguments must match its input schema. A binding with no arguments is checked as `{}`, so a missing required property is reported. A declared block action, or a method with no input schema, takes no arguments, and `{}` counts as none. A `rex.action` action's arguments must match the `args` it declares. One that declares no `args` is not checked. The client's own actions are never checked, because the client runs them and checks their arguments itself.
A diagnostic's `message` is meant for display, and its wording may change. To show a diagnostic next to the binding it is about, match on its `action` and `key` instead.

`action` is the full name of the action, exactly as it was written. `key` is spelled the same way as a binding's `keys`, with the keys of a sequence joined by a single space, such as `ctrl+a b`. A key the server cannot parse keeps the spelling the client sent. Each field is omitted when the diagnostic is not about a single action or key, such as an error loading the config file.

A warning about a binding or a removal names its `key`, and its `action` when it has one. A binding to a function has no action name, so it names only the key. A warning that an action's `args` schema is invalid names only the action.

`actions` in the reply lists the server's own actions, in that order, whatever the request declared. A block method has no `title` and its input schema as `args`. It can be bound but should not be shown in a menu. A declared block action has a `title` and no `args`. `actions` is omitted when the server offers none.

`server_actions` chooses which of the server's actions the reply lists. `all`, the default, lists the config file's actions and then every block type's. `configured` lists only the config file's actions, which suits a client that gets block actions from `block_creator.list`. `none` lists no actions. Whatever the value, bindings are checked against all of the server's actions.
`config` is present even when there is no file, because its path is what someone needs in order to create one.

`config.instance_id` identifies the server process that answered. `config.hash` is the SHA-256 of the config file and the modules it requires while it loads, or empty when there is no file. A client that stored this reply can keep using it while both values match and its own request is unchanged.
A new `instance_id` means the server restarted. Any script the client installed with `client.set_script` is gone and must be sent again.
Ask again after every `client.set_script` call, and after every `keymap_changed` event whose `hash` differs from the stored reply's.

methods.name: client.list
methods.description: List the clients connected to the server.
validation_notes: Every field is optional. A request with no fields lists every client, including command line clients such as `rex` itself.
Set `session_id` to list only the clients attached to that session. A connection that used `session.attach_all` is not attached to any session, so this never lists it.
Set `kinds` to list only the clients whose `info.kind` is one of them. A client that did not say what kind it is has no kind, so it matches no filter, not even `other`.
When no client matches, `clients` is an empty list, not null.
A client whose connection dropped stays in the list until it reconnects or its grace period ends. Until then, its `connection_state` is `lost`.
To keep a copy of this list up to date, call `session.attach_all` with `event_scope` set to `all`. The connection then receives `client_joined`, `client_left`, and `client_changed` events.

methods.name: client.perform
methods.description: Ask another client to perform one of its actions and wait for the answer.
validation_notes: Send this request on a client connection. The server tells the named client which client asked, based on the connection the request arrived on, so a client cannot claim to be another. To find a client by label or ID suffix, call `target.resolve` with the kind `client`.

The server sends the named client a `client_perform_requested` event and waits for it to answer with `client.reply`. The response's `result` is what the client returned, and is left out when the client returned `null`. `session_id` and `block_id` are passed to the client without being checked.

Requests to one client wait in line, and the client answers them one at a time in the order they arrived. `timeout_ms` counts from when the request reaches the front of the line. It defaults to 10 seconds, and a value above 30 seconds is cut to 30.

A request without `client_id` or `action`, a negative `timeout_ms`, or `args` that are not an object or that the action's schema rejects fails with `bad_request`. An ID that names no connected client fails with `not_found`.

An action the client did not declare fails with `not_supported`. A client that has declared no actions is asked anyway, and it may answer `not_supported` itself. A client that declines answers `refused`, and the message says why.

If the client is reconnecting, already has 16 requests waiting, or disconnects while the request waits, the request fails with `client_unavailable`. If the client does not answer in time, the request fails with `timeout`, and the client may still perform the action later.
When a request that named a connected client ends, the server sends a `client_performed` event with the outcome to connections that called `session.attach_all` with `event_scope` set to `all`.

methods.name: client.reply
methods.description: Report the outcome of the call that a client_call_requested event asked this client to make on another server.
validation_notes: A `client_call_requested` event asks this client to make one API call on another server, for a `client.action` request that is still running. The event has `call_id`, `server` (the `id` the request gave for that server), `method`, and `args`. Reply to every event, even when the call fails, on the connection that received it.

Set exactly one of `result` and `error`. `result` is the output of the call. Use `null` for a call with no output. `error` is `{"code": ..., "message": ...}`. If the other server returned an error, use its code and message. If the call could not be made, describe why. A reply with both or neither fails with `bad_request`.

This method is not ordered. The `client.action` request waiting for the reply holds the queue that `client.key` and `client.action` share, so the reply runs as soon as it arrives instead of waiting in that queue.
A `call_id` that no action is waiting for fails with `not_found`. This includes a call that was already answered and a call whose action timed out.

A `client_perform_requested` event asks this client to perform one of its own actions for another client's `client.perform` request. Answer it the same way, with its `call_id`. `result` is what the action returned, or `null`. If the action was not performed, set `error` with the code `not_supported`, `refused`, or `internal`. The caller receives that code unchanged. This differs from a reply to `client_call_requested`, whose code the waiting action never sees.

methods.name: client.set_label
methods.description: Set or remove the label of the calling client.
validation_notes: The request always changes the label of the client that sends it. A request that includes `client_id` fails with `bad_request`.
Spaces are trimmed from both ends of `label`. An empty label removes the current one.
A label longer than 64 bytes, or one that contains a control character, fails with `bad_request`. The error message says which rule the label breaks.
Labels do not have to be unique. Two clients with the same label are told apart by their IDs.
Labels are for people to read. The server never uses a label to decide what a client may do.

A client can also send a label when it connects, in the `client` field of its hello. That label follows the same rules, but the server fixes it instead of failing: a label that is too long is shortened to 64 bytes, and a label with a control character is removed.

methods.name: client.set_script
methods.description: Replace the Lua scripts loaded for this control client.

items.description: One key binding: the modifiers and then the key, joined with "+". The modifiers are "ctrl", "alt", "shift", and "cmd", always in that order. A logical binding names the key by its character or its unbracketed name, as in "ctrl+n" and "cmd+left". A physical binding brackets the W3C KeyboardEvent code, as in "ctrl+[KeyN]".

validation_notes: The `scripts` array is required and is the complete source set rather than an addition. Each call replaces the client's whole Lua VM, and an empty array unloads it.
A source that fails to load leaves the previous scripts running, because the replacement is built before it is published.
The request names no client and no session. A control connection owns one VM across all of its attachments, and this call always replaces that one.
`bindings` lists every key that reaches the scripts. The server offers a key to the scripts only when it matches one of `bindings`, and only for press and repeat events.

`all_keys` is never sent. An older server set it to true when a script asked to see every key, which scripts can no longer do. A client that talks to such a server should still send it every key when it is true.
That set is fixed until the next replacement. A binding the scripts add later with `rex.bind` falls outside it and never receives keys.

`diagnostics` reports the lines the server could not carry out, such as a binding for a key that cannot be spelled that way or one given an argument of the wrong type. The rest of the script still loads, so diagnostics arrive with a successful call rather than in place of one.
Installing a script changes the keymap without a `keymap_changed` event, because the client that installed it already knows. Ask `client.keymap` again after every call.

methods.name: data.connect
methods.description: Issue a single-use ticket for opening a block's data connection.
validation_notes: This control connection must be attached to `session_id` with `session.attach`. `session.attach_all` does not grant data access.
Only this control connection's principal can use the ticket. It expires after `expires_in_ms` and is used up by its first HELLO, even if the handshake fails.
`data_ref_id` is checked for syntax only. The block decides whether it exists after WELCOME.

`subprotocol` is optional. Set it to the subprotocol the data connection will use, such as `rex.data.terminal.v1`. If the connection uses a different subprotocol, the server replies with REJECT reason 0x07 before any data is sent.
If `subprotocol` is omitted, the block checks the subprotocol after WELCOME and closes the connection with status 1008 if it is not supported.
The request fails with bad request if `data_ref_id` or `subprotocol` is malformed, and with not found if the block has no data provider.

methods.name: help.all
methods.description: Describe the live Rex API surface in a structured JSON document.
validation_notes: Transports may project this document into transport-specific help views.

methods.name: hosts.list
methods.description: List the hosts this server keeps for the account.
validation_notes: A host is another Rex server that a person connects to. Every Rex server keeps a host list for its account. A device that uses a server as its home reads its hosts from that server, so all of the person's devices see the same list.

The list includes the hosts declared in the server's configuration file with `rex.host`, and the hosts that clients added with `hosts.put`. A declared host has a `source` field, such as `init.lua:4`, that says where it was declared. A host added with `hosts.put` has no `source`, and it takes the place of a declared host with the same `id`.

`diagnostics` lists warnings about the declared hosts. For example, a declared host whose label another host already uses is left out of the list, and a warning names the line that declared it. The field is omitted when there are no warnings, and `hash` does not cover it.
`hosts` is always present. It is sorted by label without regard to case, then by `id`.
Each record is returned as it was stored, including fields this server does not know. A client that sends a record back must keep them.
`hash` identifies this version of the list. `hosts.put`, `hosts.remove` and the `hosts_changed` event report the same hash for the same list.

A server started without a state directory cannot store hosts, so it returns only the declared ones. If someone breaks the stored file by editing it, the server returns `conflict` with a message that names the file.

methods.name: hosts.put
methods.description: Add a host to this server's host list, or replace the one with the same ID.
validation_notes: The device that adds a host chooses its `id`, so sending the same request again has no further effect. If the record has no `id`, the server creates one.
If the record matches the stored record in every field except `updated_at`, nothing changes and the stored record is returned.

`label` must not be empty, must not start or end with white space, and has at most 64 characters. If any other host in the list already uses the label, compared without regard to case, the server returns `conflict` with a message that names that host. For a declared host, the message also says where it was declared.

To change a declared host, put a record with its `id`. The server never writes the configuration file. It stores the record, which takes the place of the declaration. A put also undoes an earlier `hosts.remove` of the same `id`.

`endpoints` needs at least one endpoint, each in the form that the `-S` flag of `rex` accepts. Unix sockets and named pipes are not allowed, because their paths only work on the machine they belong to. A record that fails a check returns `bad_request` with a message that names the field.
The server sets `updated_at` and removes `source`. Every other field, including fields this server does not know, is stored as sent.
Every connected client receives a `hosts_changed` event when the put changes the list.
A server started without a state directory returns `not_supported`.

methods.name: hosts.remove
methods.description: Remove a host from this server's host list.
validation_notes: `removed` is true when the list had a host with the `id` before the request and has none after it. Removing a host that does not exist is not an error. `removed` is false, nothing is written, and no event is sent.

The server never writes the configuration file, so removing a declared host hides it instead. If a stored record had taken the place of a declared host, removing the record removes the host entirely. Either way, only a later `hosts.put` with the same `id` brings it back.
A server started without a state directory returns `not_supported`.
An `id` that is not a valid host record ID returns `bad_request`.
Every connected client receives a `hosts_changed` event when a record is removed.

methods.name: server.apple.grant_file_access
methods.description: Make files a Mac app was given readable by this server and its shells.
validation_notes: Local-only: the method is accepted only over the server's Unix socket.
`token` is a read extension from macOS's `sandbox_extension_issue_file`. The server redeems it only when it cannot already open `path`.

Each file gets one result, in request order. `readable` means the server could already open the path, `granted` that it redeemed the token and can now, and `denied` that it still cannot; `message` says why.
A relative path is `denied`. A request naming more than 256 files fails with `bad_request`.
Access lasts until the server exits. A client that sees `denied`, or an outcome it does not know, should copy the file somewhere the server can read instead.
This method is accepted only on connections arriving over the server's local Unix socket.

methods.name: server.config_reload
methods.description: Read the account's config file again and tell every client to ask for its keymap.
validation_notes: `generation` advances on every load, including one that failed, and is the `config.generation` the next `client.keymap` reports.
A load that fails keeps the bindings of the last load that succeeded and reports the failure as a diagnostic.
The diagnostics are the config file's own. A binding for an unknown action or an unbinding that reaches nothing depends on the asking client and arrives from `client.keymap`.

Every connected client receives a `keymap_changed` event with the new generation and the file's `hash`. A client whose last `client.keymap` reply came from the same `instance_id` with the same hash can keep its keymap.
This method is accepted only on connections arriving over the server's local Unix socket.

methods.name: server.status
methods.description: Return Rex server identity, current session activity, and the loaded configuration.
validation_notes: The request body may be omitted entirely because the method takes no arguments.
The opaque `instance_id` distinguishes PID reuse and server replacement.

`host_id` is an opaque token identifying the machine and user the server runs as. Two servers report equal tokens only when they see the same files. It is omitted when the server has no state directory. Treat a missing or different token as a different host and infer nothing else from the value.
`config` is always present. Its `generation` and `hash` match the `config` values in a `client.keymap` reply taken at the same moment.

`config.hash` is empty when there is no configuration file. A client that stored a keymap compares `config.hash` and `instance_id` with the values it stored, and calls `client.keymap` again only if either one differs.
`tailscale` appears only when the server host supports the embedded tailnet node.
`tailscale.account.login_name` is the Tailscale login for the account that enrolled the node. It is usually an email address and is for display only.
`tailscale.tailnet_name` is the admin-defined tailnet name. When no display name is configured, it contains the tailnet domain.
`tailscale.allow_tailnet_members` reports whether any tailnet member may connect. False restricts access to the account that enrolled the node.

`tailscale.https.state` is `pending` or `available`. The tailnet serves HTTPS only, and is reachable only when available. The HTTPS block is omitted while Tailscale is disabled or when an older server cannot report it.
`tailscale.error` explains why tailnet serving stopped after a listener failure. The next enable clears it.
`tailscale.https.url` appears only when HTTPS is available and the MagicDNS name is known.

methods.name: server.tailscale.disable
methods.description: Stop tailnet serving and keep the saved login.
validation_notes: The request body may be omitted because the method takes no arguments.
Disabling closes tailnet connections but does not stop sessions.
Use server.tailscale.logout to sign out and forget the active device.
Calling the method while tailnet serving is already disabled succeeds without changing saved login state.
This method is accepted only on connections arriving over the server's local Unix socket.

methods.name: server.tailscale.enable
methods.description: Enable serving the Rex API over the tailnet on a running server.
validation_notes: The request body may be omitted; `hostname` only selects the device name when this call constructs the node.
`allow_tailnet_members` defaults to false, which restricts callers to the Tailscale account that enrolled the node.
Enabling an already-enabled node updates its access policy without restarting it.

`auth_key` optionally enrolls a node constructed by this call without the browser flow. It is one-shot: the server never logs or stores it, and enrollment persists in the node's state directory, so later enables need no key. An already-enabled node ignores it.

A never-enrolled node without a valid `auth_key` starts Tailscale's normal authentication flow; the login URL appears in `auth_url` and the server log. A rejected key degrades to that same flow, observable as the `needs_login` state.

`advertise_tags` optionally lists ACL tags, each of the form `tag:name`, that a node constructed by this call requests when it enrolls. Tags give the node a machine identity in the tailnet's policy. The enrolling key or OAuth client must be permitted to grant them. Like `auth_key`, an already-enabled node ignores them. An invalid tag fails the call.
HTTPS binding is asynchronous: `https.state` remains `pending` until the certificate-backed listener becomes `available` or degrades to `unavailable`.
This method is accepted only on connections arriving over the server's local Unix socket.

methods.name: server.tailscale.login
methods.description: Ask Tailscale for a sign-in link for the enabled node.
validation_notes: Enable the node before requesting login.
After a successful request, an empty auth_url is not an error. The link arrives later in a status event, so keep listening for status events.
Request failures and caller cancellation return errors.
This method is accepted only on connections arriving over the server's local Unix socket.

methods.name: server.tailscale.logout
methods.description: Sign the node out of Tailscale and stop tailnet serving.
validation_notes: The request body may be omitted because the method takes no arguments.
A failed logout leaves the node running so the caller can retry.
If already disabled, logout succeeds without changing saved login state.
This method is accepted only on connections arriving over the server's local Unix socket.

methods.name: server.tailscale.rename
methods.description: Rename the enabled Tailscale node in place.
validation_notes: The node must be enabled.
The hostname is one DNS label: 1 to 63 ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens, with no leading or trailing hyphen.
The returned dns_name may still contain the old name. Watch status events for the new name.
This method is accepted only on connections arriving over the server's local Unix socket.

methods.name: server.version
methods.description: Return Rex build metadata for this server process.
validation_notes: The request body may be omitted entirely because the method takes no arguments.
`rex_version` matches the compact identifier printed by `rex version`.

methods.name: server.whoami
methods.description: Return the caller's identity and the account running the server.
validation_notes: The request body may be omitted entirely because the method takes no arguments.
`principal.kind` is `peer` for a caller identified by Unix socket credentials, `tailscale` for a caller identified through Tailscale, or `anonymous` for a caller admitted without identification.
`principal.transport` describes how the caller originally reached Rex. A login server preserves it when forwarding to an account server.
`principal.display` is a readable name for logs. It is never a stable identifier: compare `uid` for a peer or `user_id` for a tailnet caller.

`uid`, `gid`, and `pid` appear only for a peer. `user_id`, `login_name`, `node`, and `tags` appear only for a tailnet caller, and a non-empty `tags` list means that caller is a tagged machine rather than a person.
`principal.path` lists the route to this server. A `login-server` entry marks forwarding to an account server. The path is diagnostic information.
The principal is fixed when the control connection opens and remains the same for its lifetime.
`account` is the operating system username the server runs as. It may differ from the caller's name and is omitted when unknown.

methods.name: session.attach

bounds.description: [x, y, w, h] in normalized coordinates

methods.name: session.attach_all

The session list is a snapshot taken when delivery starts. Reconcile it with later events using the response frame's `seq`.
Events arrive in sequence without gaps. If queued payloads would exceed 8 MiB, the server closes the connection rather than dropping events, and the client reconnects for a fresh snapshot.

methods.name: session.bootstrap

bounds.description: [x, y, w, h] in normalized coordinates

rect.description: [x, y, w, h] in normalized coordinates

Each `session_view_changed` event contains the revision produced by its change. Request `session.view` when that revision is newer than this bootstrap view.

`client_id` is present even when no sessions are attached.

methods.name: session.create

methods.name: session.float_block

`bounds` must be finite, have positive width and height, and fit completely within the unit square.

If there is no previous pane, focus and the returned revision are unchanged.

methods.name: session.focus_previous_window

If there is no previous window, focus and the returned revision are unchanged.
Fails if the session has no focused window.
Fails with not found if `session_id` does not identify a live session.

methods.name: session.focus_window
methods.description: Move focus to the requested window, keeping that window's focused block. The response's `revision` is the session structural revision after the mutation, unchanged when the mutation is a no-op.

Activates the window and dispatches focus events to its focused block.
Activating the already-active window returns the current revision without changing it.

`removed_split_id` identifies the source leaf's destroyed parent split; it is omitted when the source was detached or was the root of its layer.

Moving the last block out of a floating layer removes that layer.

An already-satisfied order is a successful no-op.

methods.name: session.own_block
methods.description: Claim blocks for the calling client.

Focus, geometry, and block sizes are preserved.

methods.name: target.complete
methods.description: List target labels, ordinals, and short IDs that match a prefix.
validation_notes: The `kinds`, `context`, and `scope` fields accept the same values and follow the same restrictions as `target.resolve`.
To complete a client name, send `{"kinds": ["client"], "prefix": "st"}`. Clients contribute label and `id` completions, and each target's `where` names the program, such as `Rex.app 1.6.0`.
The trimmed prefix is matched case-insensitively against stored labels. Label completions preserve the stored text.
Windows contribute decimal ordinal completions whose text starts with the prefix. An empty prefix matches every ordinal.
When the prefix is empty or hexadecimal, every requested resource whose six-character short ID starts with it contributes an `id` completion.
A resource may produce more than one completion when its label, ordinal, or short ID begins with the same prefix.
A session or window scope that does not resolve returns an empty `completions` list rather than an error.
Completions are grouped by the order of `kinds`. Within each kind, labels are sorted case-insensitively, followed by ascending ordinals and sorted IDs.
Detached blocks are included when they remain in the selected scope.

methods.name: target.resolve
methods.description: Resolve resource queries against the server's live resources.
validation_notes: The `kinds` field must contain one or more unique values from `session`, `window`, `block`, and `client`. `client` must be the only kind.

To name a connected client, such as Rex.app, send `{"kinds": ["client"], "queries": ["studio"]}`. A client matches by full ID, label, or ID suffix. Clients have no ordinals. The result's `target` includes `client_id`, and its `where` names the program, such as `Rex.app 1.6.0`. A client request may set `scope.session` to consider only clients attached to that session. It may not set `scope.window`.
An empty client query selects `context.client_id` if that client is still connected, and otherwise the only connected app. A command line client is never chosen by default.
The `queries` field must contain at least one query. Each query produces one result in request order.
The `not_found` and `ambiguous` statuses are query results, not request errors.

Rex matches each query against all requested resource types in this order: full ID, case-insensitive exact label, positive ordinal, then a 4-32 character hexadecimal ID suffix. It stops at the first category that has a match.
A full ID searches only resources of the type named by its prefix. If that type is absent from `kinds`, the result is `not_found`. Rex does not try the text as a label or ID suffix.
Labels, ordinals, and ID suffixes may be ambiguous across resource types. Every ambiguous candidate includes `kind` so callers can distinguish them.
Labels take precedence over ordinals and ID suffixes. Use a full ID or a longer suffix to select an ID explicitly.
Only windows have ordinals. A window's ordinal is its one-based position in the session's window order.
An empty session query first uses a live `context.session_id`, then selects the sole session. If no sessions exist, the status is `not_found`. If multiple sessions exist, the status is `ambiguous`.
A request whose `kinds` include `session` must omit `scope`. A request whose `kinds` include `window` must omit `scope.window`.
Window and block searches may set `scope.session`. The value follows the same matching rules as a session query. If the scope does not resolve, every result reports that failure.
Block-only requests may also set `scope.window`. Rex resolves the session scope first, then resolves the window within those sessions. Only blocks in the resolved window are considered.
When `scope.session` is absent, window and block resolution use a live `context.session_id`, the only live session, or all live sessions, in that order.

An empty window query selects the window containing `context.block_id`. If the block is absent or stale, it selects the session's active window. An empty query is ambiguous when resolution includes multiple sessions.

An empty block query selects a live `context.block_id` when available. Otherwise it selects the focused block in the default window. When `scope.window` is set, it selects the focused block in that window.
Block results include detached blocks. For a detached block, `where` is `detached` or `detached in <session>`. For a placed block, it is `window N` or `window N of <session>`.
When several kinds are requested, an empty query uses the default for the most specific requested kind: block before window before session.
